lead: A spectral signature is the curve of reflectance against wavelength for a surface. Vegetation, soil and water absorb and scatter light differently, so each has a different curve. A sensor records radiance in a few bands; compare those values with known curves and you can tell crop from bare field from pond. This is the basis of land-cover mapping, crop monitoring and water mapping from satellites. The curve is measured as reflectance, a ratio from 0 to 1 or a percentage, so it is independent of the sun's brightness at the moment of measurement.
prereq: You need: reflectance and atmospheric effects from energy interactions, and band wavelengths from the spectrum.

blocks.text: Reflectance ρ(λ) is the fraction of light arriving at a surface that the surface sends back at wavelength λ. Wavelength λ is the distance between wave crests, measured here in micrometres (µm). Reflectance has no unit; write it as 0 to 1 or as a percentage. A spectral signature is a plot of ρ against λ from 0.4 µm to 2.5 µm. The visible part is 0.4–0.7 µm. The reflective infrared runs from 0.7 to 2.5 µm. It is split into the near-infrared (NIR), about 0.7–1.3 µm, and the shortwave infrared (SWIR), about 1.3–2.5 µm.

Why a curve and not one number: every material absorbs some wavelengths and scatters others. Absorption by pigments, water or minerals makes dips. Scattering by leaf cells, sand grains or suspended particles makes broad highs. The shape, not one band, identifies the surface. A satellite with a few bands samples this curve at fixed wavelengths; the sampled values are the measurements you classify in digital image processing.

sections.h3: Vegetation: pigments and the red edge

blocks.text: Chlorophyll absorbs blue light near 0.45 µm and red light near 0.67 µm for photosynthesis. It absorbs green near 0.55 µm less strongly, so a leaf has a small green peak: reflectance near 12% in the figure, against about 5% in blue and red. The big feature is the red edge: between about 0.68 µm and 0.75 µm reflectance rises steeply, from about 5% to 45% in the figure.

From about 0.75 to 1.3 µm, on the near-infrared plateau, a healthy leaf is bright. The cause is internal cell structure: light enters the leaf, bounces between cell walls and air spaces, and much of it leaves again. Pigments do not absorb NIR. A dense crop can reflect 40–50% or more. Beyond about 1.3 µm leaf water takes over: bands near 1.4 µm and 1.9 µm are deep dips, and the curve is near 30% at 1.6 µm and 18% at 2.2 µm in the figure.
Stressed or sparse vegetation has lower NIR and higher red, so the red edge weakens. This is why vegetation indices use red and NIR together.

Soil has a smooth curve that rises slowly from visible to shortwave infrared: 10% at 0.45 µm, 18% at 0.66 µm and 33% at 2.2 µm in the figure for dry soil. There are no sharp pigment bands. Moisture lowers the whole curve because water absorbs; organic matter darkens it; iron oxides raise red and lower blue; texture sets brightness. Dry sand is bright; wet clay is dark.

Clear water is brightest in blue (8–9% at 0.40–0.45 µm in the figure), falls through green and red, and is almost black in NIR (2% at 0.83 µm, 1% at 1.1 µm). Water absorbs NIR strongly, so ponds and rivers are dark in NIR images. Turbidity from suspended sediment raises visible reflectance, especially red. Algae add chlorophyll, which can create a green peak and red absorption. Snow is very bright in the visible and drops in shortwave infrared because ice absorbs there.

blocks.where: ρ<sub>NIR</sub> is the near-infrared reflectance and ρ<sub>red</sub> is the red reflectance; both are unitless fractions from 0 to 1. NDVI runs from −1 to +1.

blocks.text: High NIR and low red give values near +1 for green vegetation. Soil gives a low positive value; water gives zero or negative. Other indices are SAVI, EVI, NDWI and NDBI. A spectral library stores measured curves with labels and metadata; matching compares an image spectrum to library entries.

spec.aria: Reflectance in percent against wavelength from 0.4 to 2.5 micrometres. Vegetation is low in blue and red with a small green peak, rises steeply at the red edge to about 50 percent, then falls with dips near 1.45 and 1.95 micrometres. Dry soil rises smoothly from 8 to about 33 percent. Clear water falls from 9 percent in blue to almost zero beyond 0.8 micrometre. Two shaded vertical strips mark the red and near-infrared bands, with dots where each curve crosses them.

examples.question: Read the band values plotted as dots in the figure: in the red band (0.63–0.69 µm) vegetation 0.05, dry soil 0.18, clear water 0.04; in the NIR band (0.76–0.90 µm) vegetation 0.50, dry soil 0.22, clear water 0.02. (a) Compute NDVI for each cover. (b) The same crop on a slope facing away from the sun receives half the light, so both its band values halve. Find its NDVI. (c) Say what the results show.
steps: Formula: NDVI = (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> − ρ<sub>red</sub>) ÷ (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> + ρ<sub>red</sub>); reflectances are unitless.
(b) Shaded crop: red 0.025, NIR 0.25. NDVI = (0.25 − 0.025) ÷ (0.25 + 0.025) = 0.225 ÷ 0.275 = 0.818, the same as in sun. The halving cancels between top and bottom.

(c) The crop sits in the upper part of the −1 to +1 range, as dense green vegetation does (typical values 0.6–0.9); soil is just above zero; water is negative because it reflects more red than NIR. The ratio keeps the crop at 0.818 whether it is lit or shaded, which a single NIR value (0.50 against 0.25) cannot do.
examples.answer: NDVI is 0.818 for vegetation, 0.100 for dry soil and −0.333 for clear water, and stays 0.818 for the shaded crop. The sign and size of NDVI separate the three covers, and the ratio removes the illumination change.

traps: The green peak is not the brightest part of vegetation. NIR reflectance is much higher, so a false-colour image shows crops in red, not green.
Water is dark in NIR because water absorbs NIR strongly; it is not black in the visible. Clear water still reflects more blue than red.
NDVI is a ratio, not a percentage. Do not write 0.67 as 67% unless you multiply by 100, and do not swap NIR and red.
Wet soil is darker than dry soil, not brighter. Moisture absorption lowers the whole soil curve.
Snow is bright in visible bands but drops in shortwave infrared. A bright visible pixel is not automatically cloud or sand.

quiz.q: What causes the small green peak near 0.55 µm in a leaf curve?
quiz.a: Chlorophyll absorbs blue (near 0.45 µm) and red (near 0.67 µm) strongly but green less strongly, so reflectance rises a little near 0.55 µm, to about 12% against 5%.

quiz.q: Why is healthy vegetation bright in the near-infrared?
quiz.a: Light enters the leaf and scatters between cell walls and air spaces. Pigments do not absorb NIR, so much of that light leaves the leaf again.

quiz.q: A pixel has red reflectance 0.20 and NIR reflectance 0.60. Compute its NDVI.
Pixel A has red 0.12 and NIR 0.45. Pixel B has red 0.22 and NIR 0.30. Compute both NDVI values and say which pixel is more likely vegetation.
Name two water absorption bands in a leaf spectral curve.
Why do ponds and rivers appear dark in a near-infrared image?
quiz.a: Water absorbs NIR strongly, so very little NIR energy leaves the water surface and reaches the sensor.

quiz.q: Why can turbid water have higher visible reflectance than clear water but still be dark in NIR?
quiz.a: Suspended sediment scatters visible light back, raising visible reflectance. Water itself still absorbs NIR strongly, so NIR reflectance stays low.

beyond: Not for the exam. Satellite missions such as Sentinel-2 and Landsat provide free multispectral bands for these curves. Crop insurance and drought monitoring use NDVI time series. Water-quality agencies use turbidity and chlorophyll indices. Search next for 'spectral library', 'red edge position', 'NDVI time series', and 'hyperspectral unmixing'.
